drafts.title: Adobe Stock is rejecting AI images without C2PA manifests — most AI creators have never generated one
drafts.content:
Discovered this the annoying way: Adobe Stock started bouncing AI-generated image submissions earlier this year. After some digging, the issue was missing C2PA provenance metadata — a JSON manifest embedded in the file that declares what created it.

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) is backed by Adobe, Microsoft, Google, BBC, Intel, Sony, OpenAI, and roughly 2,000 others. It's the technical standard for declaring whether content is AI-generated. Adobe Stock reads it automatically. LinkedIn started surfacing it in 'About this image' popups. EU AI Act enforcement for synthetic media disclosure hits fully in August 2026.

The problem: if you're generating images with Midjourney, local Stable Diffusion, or anything outside Firefly's web app, you're getting zero C2PA metadata by default. The tooling to add it yourself used to require running a Rust CLI (c2patool) with a JSON config file.

Built a browser-based version of this. Upload your image, fill in 3 fields (creator name, generative tool, training data assertion), download the manifest-embedded version. Runs offline, image never leaves your device.

https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/c2pa-manifest-generator/blog/adobe-microsoft-bbc-every-ai-image-needs-c2pa-label-most-creators-never-heard-of-it-2026/

Built a browser-based C2PA manifest generator after watching Adobe Stock reject AI-generated image submissions for missing provenance metadata.

C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) is the technical standard backed by Adobe, Microsoft, Google, BBC, Intel, Sony, OpenAI et al. for declaring how content was created. drafts.title: I ran 100 AI pickup lines past 40 real dating app users. 3 worked. Here's the pattern.
drafts.content:
Spent a week generating and testing AI pickup lines with a panel of 40 active dating-app users. Rated each line: would reply / forgettable / would not reply.

97 out of 100 failed. The 3 that worked shared one thing: they referenced something specific from the person's profile rather than being generic openers.

The 'clever' category (wordplay, puns, witty references) got 0 positive responses. Panel feedback was consistent: engineered cleverness reads as a performance, not genuine interest.

Full breakdown with the actual lines and panel quotes: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/ai-pickup-lines/blog/i-made-an-ai-write-100-pickup-lines-the-3-that-worked-made-me-question-everything-2026/

I just realized: the problem with bad openers on dating apps is the same problem as bad cold emails.

I ran 100 AI pickup lines past 40 real users. 97 failed. The 3 that worked referenced something specific about the recipient.

The AI didn't make bad pickup lines good. It made specific observations into well-constructed sentences. The specificity still had to come from the human.

This applies directly to sales, networking, and any first-touch message you write. Generic is not a style. It's a refusal to do the work of paying attention.
